title: On the Impossibility of SNARGs with Short CRS (or: Revisiting Gentry-Wichs Barrier in the Non-adaptive Setting)
abstract:
We study the inherent barriers to constructing non-adaptively sound succinct non-interactive arguments (SNARGs) for NP with a CRS whose length is sublinear in the witness length. Our results cover both the standard SNARGs and SNARGs with an additional updatable feature (i.e. incrementally verifiable computation for NP).

- For updatable SNARGs, we show a black-box separation from falsifiable assumptions for uniform polynomial-time reductions, assuming sub-exponential hardness of learning with error.
- For general SNARGs, we show a black-box separation from falsifiable assumptions for non-uniform polynomial-time reductions that only non-adaptively make an instance-size-independent number of queries to the adversary, assuming the existence of sub-exponentially secure super-bit generators. We observe that all known SNARG constructions from polynomial hardness of standard assumptions have 1-query soundness reductions. Thus, our result complements existing constructions.

Previously, the seminal work [Gentry-Wichs, STOC'11] showed a black-box separation of SNARGs from falsifiable assumptions in the adaptive soundness setting. We explore whether any barriers exist in the non-adaptive setting. To obtain our result, we derive a simulation lemma for unbounded polynomial-length auxiliary inputs assuming super-bit generators.

                                           Abstract

arguments (SNARGs) for NP with a CRS whose length is sublinear in the witness length. Our
results cover both the standard SNARGs and SNARGs with an additional updatable feature
(i.e. incrementally verifiable computation for NP).
   • For updatable SNARGs, we show a black-box separation from falsifiable assumptions for
     uniform polynomial-time reductions, assuming sub-exponential hardness of learning with
     error.
   • For general SNARGs, we show a black-box separation from falsifiable assumptions for
     non-uniform polynomial-time reductions that only non-adaptively make an instance-size-
     independent number of queries to the adversary, assuming the existence of sub-exponentially
     secure super-bit generators. We observe that all known SNARG constructions from poly-
     nomial hardness of standard assumptions have 1-query soundness reductions. Thus, our
     result complements existing constructions.
   Previously, the seminal work [Gentry-Wichs, STOC’11] showed a black-box separation of
SNARGs from falsifiable assumptions in the adaptive soundness setting. We explore whether

1   Introduction
Succinct non-interactive arguments (SNARGs) allow a prover to convince a verifier of the truth of a
statement through a short, single-round message. The standard setting for SNARGs is the common
reference string (CRS) model, where a trusted setup algorithm generates a CRS and shares it with
both the prover and the verifier. SNARGs have a wide range of applications, including delegation
of computation [GKR15], verifying distributed computation [Val08; CT10], private information
retrieval [BDKP22], zero-knowledge [Kiy22], blockchain [BCG+14]. Beyond cryptography, it has
been used to establish the cryptographic hardness of PPAD [CHK+19; KPY20; JKKZ21; KLV23].
    Following the seminal work of Micali [Mic00], which constructed SNARGs in the random or-
acle model, a long line of research [KRR13; KRR14; BHK17; BKKSW18; KPY19; CJJ21; KVZ21;
CJJ22; HJKS22; WW22; KLVW23; CGJJZ23] has aimed to construct SNARGs from well-studied, fal-
sifiable hardness assumptions [Nao03]. Notably, it is known how to build SNARGs for NP under
well-studied cryptographic assumptions such as indistinguishability obfuscation [SW21; WW24b;
WZ24; WW24a] or witness encryption with polynomial-size Extended Frege proof of correctness
[JKLM25]. However, all prior constructions of SNARGs for NP from well-studied assumptions
have a long CRS whose length grows with the NP witness size. This leads to the following ques-
tion:

      Is there any fundamental barrier to constructing SNARGs for NP from standard assumptions,
                      with a short CRS whose length is sublinear in the witness size?

    A short CRS is a natural requirement of succinctness in SNARGs. In practice, SNARGs typically
require a distributed “ceremony” protocol to generate the CRS. A shorter CRS can reduce the cost
of this setup phase and also improve the efficiency of the prover and verifier.

Gentry-Wichs Barrier. Previously, the seminal work by Gentry and Wichs [GW11] showed that
SNARGs for NP cannot be constructed from any falsifiable assumptions, assuming a black-box
soundness reduction and the SNARG is adaptively sound. As observed in [CGKS23], if the reduc-
tion preserves the security parameter of the underlying falsifiable assumption, the Gentry–Wichs
impossibility result also applies in the long CRS setting. However, Gentry-Wichs impossibility re-
sult crucially relies on adaptive soundness, where the cheating prover may choose the instance after
observing the CRS.

This Work: Non-adaptive Soundness. In this work, we investigate whether any inherent barrier
still exists in the non-adaptive soundness setting. In this setting, the CRS is generated independently
of the instance selected by the adversary. This is a weaker notion than adaptive soundness, as it
is implied by the latter. Nevertheless, non-adaptive soundness suffices for many applications in
which the instance is chosen independently of the CRS. Moreover, non-adaptive soundness can be
generically upgraded to adaptive soundness using complexity leveraging, although this comes at
the cost of increasing the proof length with the instance size.
     This leads to the central question of this work:

             Is there an inherent barrier to constructing SNARGs for NP with a short CRS
                    that satisfy non-adaptive soundness from falsifiable assumptions?



                                                  1
    Proving black-box separations in the non-adaptive setting faces several critical challenges, which
stem from the following distinctions between non-adaptive and adaptive soundness reductions. In
the non-adaptive setting, since the adversary chooses the instance before the CRS is generated, the
reduction can run the adversary multiple times with different CRS on the same instance. This re-
duction strategy resembles rewinding, which is typically not possible in the adaptive setting. More-
over, in the non-adaptive setting, the reduction can exploit non-uniform advice that arbitrarily
depends on the instance, as shown in [JKLV24], whereas in the adaptive setting, this is impossible
since the instances are chosen adaptively. Without these two challenges, Gentry-Wichs [GW11]
can extend directly to the non-adaptive setting for 1-query, uniform reductions.
    Our work investigates the inherent barriers for both the standard SNARG notion and SNARGs
with an additional feature—updatability.

Updatable SNARGs (i.e. IVC for NP). Updatable SNARGs are defined in the following setting.
Consider a nondeterministic computation st0 → st1 → st2 → . . . → stT , where in the i-th step, one
runs a nondeterministic machine with some witness wi on the current state sti and produces the
next state sti+1 . We say a SNARG is updatable, if given the initial state st0 , a state sti , a proof πi that
sti is reachable via i-step nondeterministic computation, and the i-th witness wi , the prover can ef-
ficiently transform πi into a proof πi+1 that the state sti+1 is reachable via a (i+1)-step computation,
without recomputing everything from scratch.
     This notion was initially introduced for proving deterministic computation and is known as
incrementally verifiable computation (IVC) [Val08]. Recently, IVC has been implicitly extended to
support nondeterministic computation in concretely efficient IVC schemes [KST22; KS22; KS23;
KS24], and the recent work [DJJ+25] constructed IVC for NP with CRS length growing with the
single-step witness from standard assumptions.
     In the broader context, the updatable feature of SNARGs has been extensively studied for ver-
ifying distributed computation. Indeed, it can be viewed as a special case of proof-carrying data
[CT10] and recursive composition [BCCT13]. These techniques are particularly attractive for con-
cretely efficient SNARG constructions (e.g. [BGH19; BCMS20]), as their prover preserves the time
and space complexity of the underlying computation, and is a common “bootstrap” technique to
reduce the CRS size [BCCT13]. The impossibility we obtain in the updatable setting also implies
the impossibility of those more general settings.
     In this work, we focus on updatable SNARGs whose CRS length and proof length are both suc-
cinct, smaller than the intermediate-state size or the length of single-step witnesses. We consider
non-adaptive soundness for updatable SNARGs, where the initial state and the final state of the
computation must be chosen independently of the CRS.

1.1   Our Results
We consider both standard SNARGs and SNARGs with an additional, updatable feature. We begin
with the updatable SNARG setting (IVC for NP):

Theorem 1.1 (Impossibility for Updatable SNARGs, Informal Version of Theorem 4.5). Assuming
sub-exponential hardness of Learning with Errors, there does not exist an updatable SNARG for
NP (i.e. IVC for NP) that satisfies non-adaptive soundness, has a CRS whose length is independent
of the length of the instance and witness, and has a polynomial-time black-box uniform soundness
reduction to falsifiable assumptions.                                                          ♢

Remark 1 (CRS and Proof Lengths v.s. Instance Length). Similar to Gentry-Wichs, our impossi-
bility naturally extends to the setting where CRS length and proof length depends on the instance
length, by assuming stronger assumptions. In both this work and Gentry-Wichs, the requirement
is that 2O(|crs|+|π|) needs to be less than the hardness of the language, i.e. an adversary running in
time 2O(|crs|+|π|) should not distinguish yes instances from no instances. Therefore, if the language
has exponential hardness, then we rule out |crs|, |π| = o(n) (n is instance size); if the language has
sub-exponential hardness, then we rule out |crs|, |π| = O(nc ) for some c ∈ (0, 1).                 ♢

    Falsifiable assumptions [Nao03] are assumptions that can be formulated as an interactive game
between a challenger and an adversary. In this framework, the challenger generates a challenge,
and the adversary attempts to solve it. The assumption is considered falsifiable, if the challenger
runs in polynomial-time—so any successful adversary serves as a piece of evidence against the
assumption. All standard cryptographic assumptions—such as factoring or Learning With Er-
rors—are captured by falsifiable assumptions.

Non-Uniform Reduction. Our Theorem 1.1 focuses on uniform soundness reductions. We then
turn to the question of whether any inherent barrier remains when allowing non-uniform reductions.
In this setting, the reduction algorithm is allowed to take non-uniform advice—an arbitrary string
that may depend on the instance, but independent of the adversary. Indeed, recent work [JKLV24;
JKLM25] has shown that non-adaptively sound SNARGs can be achieved by using non-uniform
reductions for some subclasses of NP from standard assumptions. In the setting of non-uniform
reductions, we consider general SNARGs and obtain the following theorem:
Theorem 1.2 (Impossibility for General SNARGs, Informal Version of Theorem 5.10). Assuming
the existence of a sub-exponentially secure super-bit generator, there does not exist a SNARG for
NP that satisfies non-adaptive soundness, has a polynomial-time black-box non-uniform soundness
reduction to falsifiable assumptions that only makes non-adaptive query to the adversary, whose
CRS size, proof size, and reduction query complexity are independent of the length of the instance
and witness.                                                                                    ♢

    Our result relies on the existence of super-bit generators. Rudich introduced the super-bit gen-
erator as a natural extension of pseudorandom generators secure against NP adversaries, in the
context of the natural proofs barrier [RR97]. The super-bit generator can be viewed as an average-
case analog of the widely believed complexity conjecture coNP ̸⊆ NP. In his original work, Rudich
proposed a candidate construction based on the subset-sum problem. Recently, [CL24] proposed
another candidate of super-bit generators based on lattice assumptions.


On Query-bounded Reductions. Our Theorem 1.2 considers reduction algorithms with a small
number of non-adaptive queries to the adversary. While such soundness reduction may appear
limited at first glance, we observe that all known SNARG constructions from polynomial-time stan-
dard assumptions, such as [CJJ21; CJJ22; BBKLP23; JKLV24], in fact only rely on 1-query soundness
reductions.
    Hence, we view our non-adaptive-query-bounded impossibility result as capturing the limi-
tations of the soundness reduction techniques used in the literature. Namely, our result suggests
that, in order to achieve SNARGs for NP with a short CRS and proof from polynomial hardness of
falsifiable assumption—even with non-adaptive soundness—one must rely on either a soundness
reduction with large query complexity or adaptive queries, or non-black-box reduction.

      We defer more detailed discussion of 1-query nature of existing reductions to Section 2.4.

On Polynomial-time Reductions and Prior Works of SNARGs for NP. Both our results Theo-
rem 1.1 and Theorem 1.2 consider reductions runs in polynomial time. The reader may wonder
whether a reduction with a much larger runtime could circumvent our impossibility result. We
next explain the main barrier to such an approach.
    Indeed, in the prior works of SNARGs for NP from indistinguishability obfuscation (iO) or
witness encryption 1 [SW21; WW24b; WZ24; WW24a; JKLM25], when iO and witness encryption
are instantiated from falsifiable assumptions [JLS21; JLS22; RVV24], the resulting constructions
can be interpreted as having a reduction that runs in time exponential in the NP witness length,
and thereby circumventing Gentry-Wichs. However, the security of these SNARGs inherently rely
on complexity leveraging, which forces the security parameter of the underlying cryptographic
assumptions to grow at least with the NP witness length. As a result, if the CRS contains even a
single instance of the underlying assumption (e.g. a LWE sample), its size is already large. To take
advantage of a large reduction time, one might need to develop new reduction techniques that
avoid including even a single instance of the underlying assumption in the CRS.

More Comparison with Gentry-Wichs. The seminal work of Gentry and Wichs [GW11] proved
a black-box separation in the adaptive soundness setting, whereas our work focuses on the weaker,
non-adaptive setting. Gentry-Wichs considers general SNARGs and allows reductions that can
make multiple queries to the adversary. In contrast, our Theorem 1.1 considers updatable SNARGs
under uniform reductions, while Theorem 1.2 considers general SNARGs with non-adaptive-query-
bounded non-uniform reductions. Additionally, the original Gentry-Wichs impossibility result as-
sumes a short CRS that is a fixed polynomial in the security parameter to handle non-security
parameter preserving reductions. But as observed in [CGKS23], Gentry-Wichs also applies in the
long CRS setting when the CRS can grow with the NP instance length and witness length. All of
our results, by contrast, assume that the CRS length is short.

1.2     More Related Works
Updatable SNARGs (IVC) for P. Although constructing updatable SNARGs for NP remains a
hard task, it is well-understood on how to construct updatable SNARGs for P (IVC) [DGKV22;
PP22], from standard cryptogrpahic assumptions including learning with errors (LWE), a combi-
nation of quadratic residuosity (QR) and decisional Diffie-Hellman (DDH), or the DLIN assump-
tion on bilinear groups.

Other Impossibilities for Updatable SNARGs. [HAN23] considered updatable SNARGs for NP
in the random oracle model. They proved impossibility for updatable SNARGs with either 1) zero-
knowledge property that involves reprogramming the random oracle; 2) knowledge soundness
(and an additional structural assumption).

2     Technical Overview
Before diving into the technical details of this work, we briefly recall the Gentry–Wichs impos-
sibility result [GW11], which showed that adaptive soundness of SNARGs cannot be based on
falsifiable assumptions via black-box reductions.

2.1   Recap of Gentry-Wichs Barrier
A black-box soundness reduction is an algorithm R that uses a hypothetical adversary P as an
oracle to break the underlying falsifiable assumption. As a black-box reduction, the algorithm
RP should break the assumption as long as P breaks the soundness of the SNARG, regardless of
whether P is efficient.
    At a high level, Gentry-Wichs rules out such a black-box reduction for adaptively sound SNARGs
via the following “meta-reduction” strategy. They construct a pair of adversaries P and P where
P is a polynomial-time algorithm that always chooses instances that are in the language and fol-
lows the honest prover algorithm, whereas P runs in unbounded time and chooses instances that
are not in the language. Moreover, for any CRS, the outputs of the two adversaries P and P are
indistinguishable against any polynomial-time algorithm.
    To rule out black-box reductions, they start with the “honest” prover P that always makes the
verifier accept. Then they switch P to P and argue that P breaks the soundness. This is because
P and P are indistinguishable and hence, P also makes the verifier accept, but chooses instances
that are not in the language. Further, the correctness of the reduction implies that RP breaks the
underlying falsifiable assumption. Finally, they switch RP back to RP and argue that RP still
breaks the underlying assumption, again due to the indistinguishability of P and P. This reaches
a contradiction because we find a polynomial-time attack RP to break the underlying falsifiable
assumption.

Leakage Lemma. At the heart of the above meta-reduction proof strategy is the construction of
P whose output is indistinguishable from the honest prover algorithm P. To construct this P,
Gentry-Wichs proves the following leakage lemma. Let D, D be a pair of “hard” distributions, where
D is over L and D is over L = {0, 1}∗ \ L, and D and D are indistinguishable against circuits of size
T . For any “small leakage” π whose size is much smaller than log T , and π is allow to be arbitrarily
correlated to x ← D, there exists a “simulated” leakage π correlated with x̄ ← D, such that the joint
distributions {(x, π) : x ← D} and {(x̄, π̄) : x̄ ← D} are indistinguishable against polynomial-size
circuits.
    To apply this lemma, Gentry-Wichs takes the language L as the image of a pseudorandom
generator (PRG) and D as the distribution of a random PRG image, and D is taken as the uni-
form distribution over D. By the leakage lemma, there exists a simulated proof π for any “false”
instance x̄ sampled from D. Then the outputs of the honest P and a P that outputs π are computa-
tionally indistinguishable as desired. This completes the overview of Gentry-Wichs impossibility
for adaptively sound SNARGs.

2.2   Impossibility for Updatable SNARGs
Challenge: Ruling Out “Rewinding” Reductions. The proof strategy in Gentry-Wichs works
for adaptive soundness. However, it is unclear how to extend the idea to the non-adaptive sound-

ness setting. In this setting, after the adversary chooses the instance, the reduction algorithm can
send different CRS queries to the adversary and obtain multiple SNARG proofs for the same in-
stance. The reduction algorithm could potentially extract an entire witness from the adversary and
then prove the soundness by a proof of contradiction. This resembles the rewinding technique in
multi-round interactive proof soundness proofs. 2 To extend Gentry-Wichs to the non-adaptive
soundness setting, we need to rule out such a rewinding proof strategy.

Blueprint of Our Proof. Our intuition to rule out the above rewinding reduction strategy is that,
for a general NP language, if an instance has multiple witnesses, then the rewinding strategy seems
unlikely to work——if an honest prover chooses different witnesses based on different CRS each
time, then it’s unclear how to “stitch” the information from different SNARG proofs to form a
consistent NP witness in the reduction.
    Following this intuition, our blueprint for proving impossibility in the non-adaptive soundness
setting is as follows. We first choose an NP language L where each instance in L has multiple NP
witnesses. Then we construct a polynomial-time algorithm P for an instance x ∈ L sampled from
some distribution: Given any CRS queried by the reduction, P randomly chooses a witness of x
and uses the honest prover algorithm to generate an SNARG proof as its output. Next, we use a
series of hybrid arguments to “gradually” switch from P to an unbounded-time adversary P for
an instance x̄ ∈/ L, such that any polynomial-time oracle-algorithm D cannot distinguish DP and
DP . The number of hybrids is the same as the number of NP witnesses for x. In each hybrid, we
“puncture” one witness from x, and replace the honestly generated SNARG proof of this witness
with a simulated proof using the leakage lemma.
    Specifically, in the i-th hybrid, the instance is switched from the initial x to an instance x(i)
where the first i witnesses have already been removed in x(i) . The unbounded-time adversary P (i)
in this hybrid behaves almost the same as P, except that whenever the witness it samples falls in
the first i witnesses, the adversary P (i) answers the query from the reduction using a simulated
proof via the leakage lemma. In this way, we can switch from an honest prover P for some x ∈ L
to some unbounded prover P for some x̄ ∈    / L.

Towards Constructing NP Languages with Multiple Witnesses.                      Our initial attempt is to take a
PRG G and let the language L be

                           L = {x = (x1 , . . . , xm ) | ∃i ∈ [m] : xi ∈ Image(G)} .

The NP witness is an index i and the PRG seed for xi . If we sample all x1 , . . . , xm from the PRG
image, then we have m PRG seeds as the witnesses. However, this language does not meet our
needs directly since the number of CRS queries made by the reduction may depend on the length

more than m queries, then our intuition in the above blueprint does not hold because there will be
many collisions in the random sampling of the witnesses, and one witness may be used multiple
times to generate the proof. Now the reduction can still potentially extract an entire witness.

evasive LWE [MPV24].

2.3   Impossibility for General SNARGs
In this section, we focus on general non-adaptively sound SNARGs, without assuming any addi-
tional feature of the prover’s algorithm. We outline the techniques in our Theorem 1.2, which rules
out non-adaptive-query-bounded non-uniform black-box reductions in this setting.

Non-uniform Reduction and Non-deterministic Computation. In a non-uniform reduction, the
reduction algorithm is additionally given a polynomially long advice that arbitrarily depends on
the instance. Since the (number-bounded) queries to the adversary can always be simulated if
the language is “hard” enough, as shown in Gentry-Wichs’ leakage lemma, we can ignore the
queries for the moment. Under this view, the reduction algorithm is essentially a nondeterministic
algorithm, where the non-uniform advice can be viewed as the NP witness.
    To rule out non-uniform reductions, we need to choose a hard language L that can fool this non-
deterministic reduction algorithm. A natural candidate is the super-bit generators introduced in
[Rud97] as the analogue of PRG against nondeterministic distinguishers. The security of super-bit
generators guarantees that, any nondeterministic algorithm accepts a random string with no no-
ticeably higher probability than accepting a random super-bit generator image. Intuitively, this
assumption can be viewed as saying “uniformly random strings” do not have NP proofs “on aver-
age”. Note that in the nondeterministic setting, indistinguishability is directional. While we believe
the existence of super-bit generator, it is easy to construct a nondeterministic algorithm that accepts
a random super-bit generator image with higher probability than a random string: the algorithm
just checks if the input is in the image of the super-bit generator. Because of this reason, in the rest
of this section we adopt the notation “X → Y are indistinguishable” (which means X cannot be
accepted with noticeably higher probability than Y ) rather than “X, Y are indistinguishable” to
stress the order between distributions X, Y .
    We can let the hard language L be the set of the images of a super-bit generator. However, the
security guarantee of the super-bit generator cannot be directly applied in our setting, since so far
we have ignored the queries to the adversary. To take the queries into account, we first prove the
following leakage simulation lemma for unbounded leakage.

any polynomial-length advice Y ′ of Y , there exists a “simulated advice” X ′ possibly correlated with
X, such that X ′ , Y ′ are indistinguishable against (deterministic) polynomial-time distinguishers.♢

We prove this lemma using von Neumann’s min-max theorem [Neu28]. In our setting, X = Uℓ(n)

We only discuss black-box reductions showing the non-adaptive soundness of some IVC (and more
